blueprint.title: Delta Codec Silent Corruption
blueprint.scenario: The telemetry pipeline team shipped a large refactor of the on-disk delta-encoding library (`/app`) that compresses time-series sensor readings. The refactor touched six files and passed all 47 regression tests, but production deployments started silently producing wrong decompressed values on certain sensor feeds. A compiled reference binary (`/app/bin/refcodec`) was preserved from the last known-good release and still produces correct output. The pipeline is written in Go, and the new source lives in `/app/src/`. The Dockerfile builds a fresh `codec` binary from the refactored source.
blueprint.instruction_draft: The build is green but the refactored delta codec at `/app/src/` silently corrupts decompressed output for certain input patterns; the pre-refactor reference binary `/app/bin/refcodec` is the ground truth. Your job is to make the rebuilt `codec` binary produce byte-for-byte identical output to `refcodec` on every valid input stream. Both binaries share the same CLI: `codec compress < raw.bin > compressed.bin` and `codec decompress < compressed.bin > raw.bin`. The decompressed output of a round-trip (`compress` then `decompress`) must exactly reproduce the original input, and the compressed bytes produced by `codec` must be decompressible by `refcodec` and vice versa — cross-binary interoperability is required. Do not modify the wire format or the CLI interface.
requirements: Running `codec compress | codec decompress` on any valid input reproduces the original bytes exactly.
Files compressed by `codec` can be decompressed by `refcodec` with identical output.
Files compressed by `refcodec` can be decompressed by `codec` with identical output.
The `codec` binary must be rebuilt from `/app/src/` (the Dockerfile build step must succeed).
The CLI interface (`compress` / `decompress` subcommands reading stdin, writing stdout) is unchanged.
environment: Dockerfile FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm installs Go 1.23 via apt/manual install, copies /app, and runs `go build -o /app/bin/codec ./src/` as part of image build.
Reference binary `/app/bin/refcodec` is pre-compiled from the correct implementation and baked into the image; its source is NOT present.
Refactored Go source in `/app/src/` across ~1,400 lines in 6 files: `main.go`, `compress.go`, `decompress.go`, `delta.go`, `frame.go`, `varint.go`.

Bug 1 (data-dependent, not visible by reading): In `delta.go`, the delta-of-delta encoding for the 'XOR predictor' path uses an arithmetic right shift emulated as `int64(uint64(v) >> n)` but the refactor changed it to `v >> n` (Go's signed shift), which is correct for negative values but the refactor also silently swapped the XOR predictor branch condition — it now enters the XOR path when the value is positive and the arithmetic path when negative, the opposite of the reference. The branch condition reads naturally correct on inspection (`if delta > 0`) but the reference used `if prevDelta > 0`. This only diverges when a run of values transitions from decreasing to increasing.

Bug 2 (construction required, not visible by reading): In `frame.go`, the frame checksum was changed from CRC32/IEEE to CRC32/Castagnoli (the constant `crc32.Castagnoli` appears in the new code and seems intentional), but `decompress.go` still validates using `crc32.IEEE`. The refcodec used CRC32/IEEE for both. The codec compresses with Castagnoli and validates with IEEE — frames it writes always fail validation when read back after the interop path, but since `decompress.go` silently skips malformed frames (logs a warning, does not abort), single-stream round-trips on short inputs appear to work. Hidden tests use streams long enough to contain multiple frames.

Plausible uninvolved code: `varint.go` has a correct variable-length integer encoder/decoder (~200 lines), `main.go` has flag parsing and a benchmark subcommand, `compress.go` has LRU-based literal run detection — none are buggy.
Test data `/app/testdata/` contains 6 short sensor recordings (each < 1 MB) that all pass the existing regression suite despite both bugs.
A regression test script `/app/test_regression.sh` runs the 47 existing tests; it passes on the broken source.

Verifier generates fresh synthetic sensor streams at verify time (lengths 50k–2M samples, value ranges chosen to exercise both increasing-then-decreasing and multi-frame transitions) and compares `codec` output against `refcodec` output.
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from two interacting runtime-only defects. Bug 1 (predicate swap in delta.go) only manifests when a monotone run reverses direction — short test inputs rarely do this. Bug 2 (checksum polynomial mismatch between compress.go and decompress.go, compounded by silent frame-skip) looks like a noop on single-frame inputs but corrupts multi-frame decompression silently. Neither bug is obvious from reading: the predicate `if delta > 0` vs `if prevDelta > 0` requires knowing which variable the reference used (discoverable only by running `refcodec` on crafted inputs and observing byte-level divergence), and the CRC mismatch requires noticing that the frame-skip warning fires at all (requires long enough input to span a frame boundary). The solver must: (1) run both binaries on crafted streams and diff outputs to locate divergence points, (2) instrument or binary-inspect `refcodec` to determine the correct predicate variable (it can be inferred by bisecting inputs), (3) identify the CRC polynomial mismatch by examining the silent-skip behavior on multi-frame data.
blueprint.trap: A solver who reads `delta.go` and sees `if delta > 0` may accept it as plausible (delta-positive means value is rising, enter XOR path — sounds reasonable) and not fix it. A solver who fixes only the CRC mismatch will pass short single-frame tests but fail on multi-frame hidden inputs. A solver who fixes only the predicate swap will fail on any multi-frame input because corrupted frames are silently skipped. Both bugs must be fixed together, and they interact: with only one fixed, round-trip tests on the provided testdata still pass because the testdata is short enough to fit in one frame and avoids direction-reversal patterns.
tests: Fuzz test 1: generate 200 synthetic streams of 50k–500k int64 samples with monotone segments of 200–5000 samples alternating direction; compress with `codec`, decompress with `codec`, diff against original — must be zero.
Fuzz test 2: generate 100 streams spanning multiple frames (>128KB compressed); compress with `refcodec`, decompress with `codec` — output must match original.
Fuzz test 3: generate 100 streams spanning multiple frames; compress with `codec`, decompress with `refcodec` — output must match original.
Fuzz test 4: streams with values that stay positive throughout (stress the XOR predictor consistently) — must round-trip correctly through both binaries.
Fuzz test 5: streams with values that stay negative throughout — must round-trip correctly.
Fuzz test 6: streams that cross zero multiple times — must round-trip correctly.
Regression gate: the 47 existing tests in `/app/test_regression.sh` must still pass (ensures the solver did not break anything else).
Build gate: `go build -o /tmp/codec_check ./src/` must succeed from `/app`.

verifier_knob.name: stream_count_and_length
verifier_knob.effect: Reducing to 20 streams under 50k samples makes Bug 1 unlikely to trigger (short streams rarely reverse direction) and Bug 2 unobservable (single-frame streams). Raising to 500 streams over 5M samples makes both bugs hit with near certainty and dramatically increases verification time.

expected_failure_modes: Agent reads delta.go, finds `delta > 0` plausible, fixes only the CRC mismatch, passes provided testdata, misses hidden multi-directional-stream tests because Bug 1 is unfixed.
Agent fixes Bug 1 predicate but misses the silent frame-skip caused by CRC mismatch; long-stream cross-binary tests fail.

Agent notices the CRC constant mismatch but 'fixes' it by changing both compress and decompress to Castagnoli, which makes codec self-consistent but breaks cross-binary interoperability with refcodec (which uses IEEE).
Agent generates only short test streams to validate (matching the existing testdata length), declares success, but hidden tests use multi-frame streams.
Agent spends time on varint.go or compress.go (the uninvolved plausible-looking code) and runs out of time before locating both real bugs.

invalid_failure_risks: Both bugs are visible by direct source inspection (one-word predicate swap, mismatched CRC constants in two files) — the claim they are 'not visible by reading' is false, undermining the intended difficulty model.

The fix for Bug 1 requires knowing which variable the reference used, but since both `delta` and `prevDelta` are local variables whose names are self-documenting, an agent reading the code can infer the correct one without running any experiments.

The silent frame-skip behavior (Bug 2 interaction) could be environment-dependent if the frame-size threshold isn't deterministic or if the Go runtime/library versions differ between refcodec compilation and the test environment.

The base image is python:3.13-slim-bookworm installing Go 1.23 via apt/manual — if Go 1.23 is not available in bookworm's apt repo, the build step fails making the task unsolvable; the blueprint should pin the exact Go tarball URL.

If the solver changes compress.go and decompress.go both to Castagnoli (a listed valid-seeming but wrong fix), the verifier must clearly distinguish this from the correct fix — this works only if refcodec is truly baked in and uses IEEE, which is correct per the spec.
The 'speedrun' path finds both bugs in ~6 file reads, making genuine_difficulty score at most 2 per the rubric's stated rule about source-visible bugs.
review.reasons: Both bugs are directly visible by reading the source code (a one-word variable name change and a mismatched constant between two files), so a methodical agent solves this in ~17 commands without any binary probing or runtime inference — genuine_difficulty scores 2, failing the threshold of 4. The blueprint's own claim that the bugs are 'not visible by reading' is inaccurate: `if delta > 0` vs `if prevDelta > 0` is a named-variable difference readable in the source, and `crc32.Castagnoli` vs `crc32.IEEE` is a literal constant mismatch across two files. The difficulty design collapses because the intended hard path (run crafted inputs, binary-diff outputs, bisect) is entirely skippable.
fixes: Make Bug 1 truly runtime-only: instead of swapping a variable name (readable), encode the predicate error as a wrong arithmetic operation or off-by-one in an accumulated state variable that only diverges when inspecting intermediate memory state — e.g., an incorrect initialization of `prevDelta` to 0 vs the last frame's final delta, which requires multi-frame boundary experiments to detect.

Make Bug 2 harder to find: instead of a named constant mismatch (Castagnoli vs IEEE, obvious to grep), use a correct CRC32/IEEE but with a byte-order swap in the frame header serialization — both sides use 'IEEE' but one writes big-endian and one reads little-endian, invisible to constant-grep and requiring byte-level frame inspection.

Ensure the source of Bug 1 is not deducible from variable names alone: rename variables so that both `delta` and `prevDelta` appear semantically plausible in the predicate context, or better, make the bug a missing negation or a wrong arithmetic operator rather than a wrong variable name.
Pin the Go installation to a specific tarball URL and SHA256 in the Dockerfile to prevent build failures due to package availability on bookworm.

verdicts.reason: Both tasks involve a refactored library that silently corrupts output on inputs outside the regression test corpus, with a reference binary as ground truth, requiring cross-compatibility fixes — the core debugging pattern is identical, only the domain (delta codec vs. AES-CTR encryption) differs.
This task asks to implement a compressor from scratch following a specification, not to debug silent corruption in a refactored codebase.
This task focuses on fixing panics and meeting a latency benchmark in a Rust packet-codec service, not debugging silent output corruption against a reference binary.
This task involves building a TCP audit service with HMAC computation and database lookups, unrelated to delta-encoding or silent decompression corruption.
This task requires reverse-engineering a black-box normalizer binary and fixing a data pipeline, not debugging a refactored codec against a reference binary.
